paragraphs: Every day, people around the world drink more than two billion cups of coffee. But how did a small red fruit from the hills of Africa become one of the most popular drinks on the planet?

According to a famous legend, a goat herder in Ethiopia called Kaldi noticed that his goats became unusually lively after eating the fruit of a certain bush. Historians are not sure that the story is true, but they agree that coffee plants first grew wild in Ethiopia.

By the fifteenth century, people in Yemen were roasting the beans and making a drink from them. Religious men drank it to stay awake during long night prayers. From there, coffee spread to Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul, where the first coffee houses opened. They quickly became places to meet friends, play games, listen to music and discuss the news.

In the seventeenth century, coffee arrived in Europe. Not everyone welcomed it: some people called it "the bitter invention of Satan". Even so, coffee houses opened in Venice, London, Paris and Vienna. In London they were nicknamed "penny universities", because for the price of a cup you could listen to conversations about science, politics and business. One of them, owned by Edward Lloyd, became the famous insurance market that still carries his name.
European countries soon started growing coffee in their colonies, from Indonesia to Brazil, often using the forced labour of enslaved people. Brazil is still the world's largest producer today.

Today coffee is a huge industry, but for many small farmers life is hard, because prices change a lot from year to year. That is why some people choose "fair trade" coffee, which promises farmers a minimum price. So next time you drink a cup, remember the long journey behind it.
